claim: Mutations in the polycystin proteins, PC-1 and PC-2, result in autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) and ultimately renal failure.
source: Mutations in the polycystin proteins, PC-1 and PC-2, result in autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) and ultimately renal failure.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by the context of the manuscript.

claim: PC-1 and PC-2 enrich on primary cilia.
source: PC-1 and PC-2 enrich on primary cilia, where they are thought to form a heteromeric ion channel complex.
evidence: This is established knowledge referenced in the manuscript.

claim: PC-1 and PC-2 are thought to form a heteromeric ion channel complex.
source: PC-1 and PC-2 enrich on primary cilia, where they are thought to form a heteromeric ion channel complex.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on prior research in the field.

claim: The PC-1/PC-2 polycystin complex functions as an outwardly rectifying channel when reconstituted in the plasma membrane of mammalian cells.
source: Here we successfully reconstitute the PC-1/PC-2 complex in the plasma membrane of mammalian cells and show that it functions as an outwardly rectifying channel.
evidence: This claim is supported by whole cell patch clamp recordings presented in the manuscript (Figure 1).

claim: A soluble fragment generated from the N-terminal extracellular domain of PC-1 functions as an intrinsic agonist that is necessary and sufficient for channel activation.
source: Using both reconstituted and ciliary polycystin channels, we further show that a soluble fragment generated from the N-terminal extracellular domain of PC-1 functions as an intrinsic agonist that is necessary and sufficient for channel activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that N-terminal fragments activate polycystin channels (Figures 3, 5, 6).

claim: Autoproteolytic cleavage of the N-terminus of PC-1 produces a soluble ligand in vivo.
source: We thus propose that autoproteolytic cleavage of the N-terminus of PC-1, a hotspot for ADPKD mutations, produces a soluble ligand in vivo.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the experimental findings and known autoproteolytic cleavage of PC-1.

claim: The N-terminus of PC-1 is a hotspot for ADPKD mutations.
source: We thus propose that autoproteolytic cleavage of the N-terminus of PC-1, a hotspot for ADPKD mutations, produces a soluble ligand in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by reference to mutation databases and prior literature (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).

claim: ADPKD is the most common monogenetic disease in humans.
source: The most common monogenetic disease in humans is ADPKD; a major nephropathy characterized by renal cysts that leads to urinary tract infection, hypertension, aneurysm, and ultimately end-stage renal disease (ESRD) (Kathem et al., 2014; Harris and Torres, 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: ADPKD is characterized by renal cysts that lead to urinary tract infection, hypertension, aneurysm, and ultimately end-stage renal disease (ESRD).
source: The most common monogenetic disease in humans is ADPKD; a major nephropathy characterized by renal cysts that leads to urinary tract infection, hypertension, aneurysm, and ultimately end-stage renal disease (ESRD) (Kathem et al., 2014; Harris and Torres, 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Mutations in PC-1 (encoded by PKD1) account for 85% of ADPKD-causing mutations.
source: Mutations in one of two ciliary proteins, PC-1 (encoded by PKD1) and PC-2 (also known as TRPP1 and encoded by PKD2), account for 85% and 15% of ADPKD-causing mutations, respectively (Harris and Torres, 2009; Cornec-Le Gall et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Mutations in PC-2 (encoded by PKD2) account for 15% of ADPKD-causing mutations.
source: Mutations in one of two ciliary proteins, PC-1 (encoded by PKD1) and PC-2 (also known as TRPP1 and encoded by PKD2), account for 85% and 15% of ADPKD-causing mutations, respectively (Harris and Torres, 2009; Cornec-Le Gall et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: PC-1 is an 11 transmembrane (TM) protein of 4303 amino acids.
source: PC-1 is an 11 transmembrane (TM) protein of 4303 amino acids with a long extracellular N-terminus that contains multiple cell adhesion domains (Yoder et al., 2002; Hughes et al., 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: PC-1 has a long extracellular N-terminus that contains multiple cell adhesion domains.
source: PC-1 is an 11 transmembrane (TM) protein of 4303 amino acids with a long extracellular N-terminus that contains multiple cell adhesion domains (Yoder et al., 2002; Hughes et al., 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: PC-1 family members (PC-1L1, PC-1L2, and PC-1L3) share the same 11-TM topology but vary in the size and adhesion domain composition of their N-termini.
source: PC-1 and its family members (PC-1L1, PC-1L2, and PC-1L3) share the same 11-TM topology but vary in the size and adhesion domain composition of their N-termini (Ishimaru et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: PC-1 family members share the GPCR autoproteolysis inducing (GAIN) domain with adhesion G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs).
source: A unique feature of PC-1 family members, shared only by adhesion G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), is the GPCR autoproteolysis inducing (GAIN) domain.
evidence: This is established knowledge about protein domain structure.

claim: The GAIN domain catalyzes peptide bond hydrolysis at a GPCR proteolysis site (GPS) that is positioned proximal to the first TM helix (TM1).
source: This domain catalyzes peptide bond hydrolysis at a GPCR proteolysis site (GPS) that is positioned proximal to the first TM helix (TM1) (Araç et al., 2012; Prömel et al., 2013; Trudel et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Autoproteolysis generates two fragments: an N-terminal fragment (NTF) and a multi-TM core.
source: Autoproteolysis generates two fragments: an N-terminal fragment (NTF) and a multi-TM core (Qian et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The NTF contains multiple domains, including leucine-rich repeats, a C-type lectin (CTL) domain, immunoglobulin (Ig)-like polycystic kidney disease (PKD) repeat domains, a single low-density lipoprotein (LDL) receptor motif, and the receptor for egg jelly (REJ) domain.
source: The NTF contains multiple domains, including leucine-rich repeats, a C-type lectin (CTL) domain, immunoglobulin (Ig)-like polycystic kidney disease (PKD) repeat domains, a single low-density lipoprotein (LDL) receptor motif, and the receptor for egg jelly (REJ) domain (Hughes et al., 1995; Babich et al., 2004; Moy et al., 1996).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Mutations within the GPS site of PC-1 result in renal cyst formation.
source: While mutations within the GPS site of PC-1 result in renal cyst formation, the full functional consequences of autoproteolysis are poorly understood (Qian et al., 2002; Yu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: PC-1 and PC-2 form a 1:3 heteromer.
source: Recent studies suggest that PC-1 and PC-2 form a 1:3 heteromer (Su et al., 2018; Yu et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of a PC-1/PC-2 heteromer reveals that the 11 transmembrane helices of PC-1 are divided into two major domains: a peripheral TM1-TM5 complex and a core TM6-TM11 complex that interdigitates with three PC-2 subunits to form a TRP-like ion channel.
source: Indeed, the cryo-EM structure of a PC-1/PC-2 heteromer reveals that the 11 transmembrane helices of PC-1 are further divided into two major domains: a peripheral TM1-TM5 complex and a core TM6-TM11 complex that interdigitates with three PC-2 subunits to form a TRP-like ion channel (Su et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a cryo-EM structure study.

claim: PC-2 can form homomeric channels, following a classic homotetramer of TRP channels.
source: In addition to this PC-1/PC-2 assembly, PC-2 can form homomeric channels, following a classic homotetramer of TRP channels (Shen et al., 2016; Grieben et al., 2017; Wilkes et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: Attempts to exogenously express and record from PC-1 and/or PC-2 in whole cell recordings of mammalian cells and reconstituted lipid bilayers have yielded divergent results.
source: Attempts to exogenously express and record from PC-1 and/or PC-2 in whole cell recordings of mammalian cells (Hanaoka et al., 2000; Delmas et al., 2004; Cai et al., 2004) and reconstituted lipid bilayers González-Perrett et al., 2001 have yielded divergent results, likely due to subcellular enrichment of PC-1 and PC-2 (for a detailed discussion see Liu et al., 2018; Kleene and Kleene, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies and reviews.

claim: It remains technically challenging to study ion channel activity in primary cilia due to their small size (10−15 L, approximately the size of a bacterium).
source: In addition, despite recent advances in measuring ion channel activity in small subcellular organelles such as the cilium (Kleene and Kleene, 2012; DeCaen et al., 2013; Dong et al., 2008), it remains technically challenging to study ion channel activity in primary cilia due to their small size (10−15 L, approximately the size of a bacterium).
evidence: This is a statement about technical challenges supported by citations.

claim: Some studies suggest that PC-1 acts as a dominant-negative subunit of the heteromeric channel.
source: Some studies suggest that PC-1 acts as a dominant-negative subunit of the heteromeric channel (Su et al., 2018), whereas others suggest that it is a pore-forming subunit that fine-tunes ion selectivity (Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: Some studies suggest that PC-1 is a pore-forming subunit that fine-tunes ion selectivity.
source: Some studies suggest that PC-1 acts as a dominant-negative subunit of the heteromeric channel (Su et al., 2018), whereas others suggest that it is a pore-forming subunit that fine-tunes ion selectivity (Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: PC-1 has been shown to be dispensable for polycystin currents in ciliary membranes.
source: Moreover, PC-1 has been shown to be dispensable for polycystin currents in ciliary membranes (Liu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: PC-1 was successfully targeted to the plasma membrane of HEK293 cells by replacing its endogenous signal peptide with a strong Ig κ-chain secretion sequence followed by an HA tag (sPC-1).
source: We were able to target PC-1 to the plasma membrane of HEK293 cells (Figure 1B) and mIMCD3 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E) by replacing its endogenous signal peptide with a strong Ig κ-chain secretion sequence followed by an HA tag (sPC-1; Figure 1A, Table 1; Salehi-Najafabadi et al., 2017; Zhu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and citations.

claim: Co-expression of sPC-1 and PC-2 resulted in strong HA surface staining in HEK293 cells.
source: Co-expression of sPC-1 and PC-2 resulted in strong HA surface staining, whereas expression of sPC-1 alone resulted in only marginal surface staining, in both HEK293 cells (Figure 1B and C) and IMCD3 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: Expression of sPC-1 alone resulted in only marginal surface staining in HEK293 cells.
source: Co-expression of sPC-1 and PC-2 resulted in strong HA surface staining, whereas expression of sPC-1 alone resulted in only marginal surface staining, in both HEK293 cells (Figure 1B and C) and IMCD3 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: Co-expression of PC-2 and PC-1 with an extracellular HA tag but without the endogenous leader sequence (HAPC-1) failed to generate comparable HA surface staining.
source: Co-expression of PC-2 and PC-1 with an extracellular HA tag but without the endogenous leader sequence (HAPC-1) failed to generate comparable HA surface staining, supporting the notion that an Ig κ-secretion sequence promotes membrane localization of the complex (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: An Ig κ-secretion sequence promotes membrane localization of the PC-1/PC-2 complex.
source: Co-expression of PC-2 and PC-1 with an extracellular HA tag but without the endogenous leader sequence (HAPC-1) failed to generate comparable HA surface staining, supporting the notion that an Ig κ-secretion sequence promotes membrane localization of the complex (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental comparison shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Robust surface HA and FLAG staining only occurred when both sPC-1 and PC-2FLAG were co-expressed.
source: Robust surface HA and FLAG staining only occurred when both sPC-1 and PC-2FLAG were co-expressed, suggesting that they are shuttled simultaneously to the plasma membrane (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: sPC-1 and PC-2FLAG are shuttled simultaneously to the plasma membrane.
source: Robust surface HA and FLAG staining only occurred when both sPC-1 and PC-2FLAG were co-expressed, suggesting that they are shuttled simultaneously to the plasma membrane (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: Co-expression of sPC-1 with PC-2F604P resulted in comparable HA surface expression to sPC-1 with PC-2.
source: Similarly, co-expression of sPC-1 with PC-2 containing a recently in an oocyte expression system characterized gain of function mutation of PC-2 (PC-2F604P, Table 1; Arif Pavel et al., 2016) resulted in comparable HA surface expression (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: PC-2F604P is a gain of function mutation characterized in an oocyte expression system.
source: Similarly, co-expression of sPC-1 with PC-2 containing a recently in an oocyte expression system characterized gain of function mutation of PC-2 (PC-2F604P, Table 1; Arif Pavel et al., 2016) resulted in comparable HA surface expression (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: Only sPC-1/PC-2F604P produced constitutively active, outward rectifying currents (122.6 ± 23.0 pA/pF at +100 mV, n = 7).
source: Interestingly, only sPC-1/PC-2F604P produced constitutively active, outward rectifying currents (122.6 ± 23.0 pA/pF at +100 mV, n = 7) with a half-maximal activation voltage of +112.5 mV (Figure 1D, E and G).
evidence: This is supported by whole cell patch clamp data shown in Figure 1D, E and G.

claim: sPC-1/PC-2F604P has a half-maximal activation voltage of +112.5 mV.
source: Interestingly, only sPC-1/PC-2F604P produced constitutively active, outward rectifying currents (122.6 ± 23.0 pA/pF at +100 mV, n = 7) with a half-maximal activation voltage of +112.5 mV (Figure 1D, E and G).
evidence: This is supported by whole cell patch clamp data shown in Figure 1D, E and G.

claim: sPC-1/PC-2 yielded negligible currents at +100 mV (5.1 ± 1.0 pA/pF, n = 11).
source: sPC-1/PC-2 (5.1 ± 1.0 pA/pF, n = 11), HAPC-1/PC-2F604P (5.0 ± 2.3 pA/pF, n = 15) and PC-2F604P alone (6.4 ± 2.1 pA/pF, n = 12) yielded negligible currents at +100 mV (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by whole cell patch clamp data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: HAPC-1/PC-2F604P yielded negligible currents at +100 mV (5.0 ± 2.3 pA/pF, n = 15).
source: sPC-1/PC-2 (5.1 ± 1.0 pA/pF, n = 11), HAPC-1/PC-2F604P (5.0 ± 2.3 pA/pF, n = 15) and PC-2F604P alone (6.4 ± 2.1 pA/pF, n = 12) yielded negligible currents at +100 mV (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by whole cell patch clamp data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: PC-2F604P alone yielded negligible currents at +100 mV (6.4 ± 2.1 pA/pF, n = 12).
source: sPC-1/PC-2 (5.1 ± 1.0 pA/pF, n = 11), HAPC-1/PC-2F604P (5.0 ± 2.3 pA/pF, n = 15) and PC-2F604P alone (6.4 ± 2.1 pA/pF, n = 12) yielded negligible currents at +100 mV (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by whole cell patch clamp data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Three positively charged amino acids (R4100, R4107, and H4111) were mutated to glycine in the putative ion permeation pathway of PC-1 to create sPC-1pore.
source: To investigate the functional contribution of PC-1 to heteromeric polycystin complexes, we mutated three positively charged amino acids in the putative ion permeation pathway to the small, uncharged amino acid glycine (R4100G, R4107G, and H4111G) in order to facilitate cation permeation (sPC-1pore; Figure 1H, Table 1).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design shown in Figure 1H.

claim: sPC-1pore/PC-2F604P generated currents of 71.1 ± 5.4 pA/pF (n = 6) at +180 mV.
source: In combination with PC-2F604P, currents of 71.1 ± 5.4 pA/pF (n = 6) were generated at +180 mV (sPC-1pore/PC-2F604P; Figure 1I).
evidence: This is supported by whole cell patch clamp data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: The relative open probability of sPC-1pore/PC-2F604P at −100 mV (0.3 ± 0.0) was higher than sPC-1/PC-2F604P (0.1 ± 0.0).
source: Although the recorded current density was ~50 pA/pF smaller than for sPC-1/PC-2F604P (Figure 1J), the relative open probability at −100 mV was higher (0.3 ± 0.0 for sPC-1pore/PC-2F604P; 0.1 ± 0.0 for sPC-1/PC-2F604P), suggesting that the pore mutant resides in a more open state (Figure 1K).
evidence: This is supported by whole cell patch clamp data shown in Figure 1K.

claim: The pore mutant (sPC-1pore/PC-2F604P) resides in a more open state than sPC-1/PC-2F604P.
source: Although the recorded current density was ~50 pA/pF smaller than for sPC-1/PC-2F604P (Figure 1J), the relative open probability at −100 mV was higher (0.3 ± 0.0 for sPC-1pore/PC-2F604P; 0.1 ± 0.0 for sPC-1/PC-2F604P), suggesting that the pore mutant resides in a more open state (Figure 1K).
evidence: This is inferred from the open probability data shown in Figure 1K.

claim: PC-1/PC-2 subunits form a functional channel when reconstituted in mammalian cells.
source: Collectively, these results demonstrate that PC-1/PC-2 subunits form a functional channel when reconstituted in mammalian cells and support the notion that PC-1 subunits form part of the core channel complex.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in Figure 1.

claim: PC-1 subunits form part of the core channel complex.
source: Collectively, these results demonstrate that PC-1/PC-2 subunits form a functional channel when reconstituted in mammalian cells and support the notion that PC-1 subunits form part of the core channel complex.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in Figure 1.

claim: ADPKD-causing mutations occur with high frequency in the N-terminal region of PC-1.
source: We reasoned that the N-terminus must be a critical determinant of polycystin function because ADPKD-causing mutations occur with high frequency in this region and therefore investigated a family member with a divergent N-terminus, PC-1L3 (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by reference to mutation databases shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: sPC-1L3 co-expressed with PC-2 or PC-2F604P resulted in strong surface HA staining.
source: Substitution of PC-1L3's signal peptide with the κ IgG secretion sequence (sPC-1L3, Table 1) resulted in strong surface HA staining when co-expressed with PC-2 or PC-2F604P (Figure 2B and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and D.

claim: sPC-1L3/PC-2F604P-transfected HEK cells did not produce convincing currents (3.5 ± 0.0 pA/pF, n = 12).
source: However, we were unable to record convincing currents in sPC-1L3/PC-2F604P-transfected HEK cells (3.5 ± 0.0 pA/pF, n = 12), suggesting that, although present in the plasma membrane, the complex is inactive (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by whole cell patch clamp data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The sPC-1L3/PC-2F604P complex is inactive although present in the plasma membrane.
source: However, we were unable to record convincing currents in sPC-1L3/PC-2F604P-transfected HEK cells (3.5 ± 0.0 pA/pF, n = 12), suggesting that, although present in the plasma membrane, the complex is inactive (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of currents despite surface expression shown in Figure 2B-D.

claim: All PC-1/PC-1L3 chimeras localized to the plasma membrane when co-expressed with PC-2F604P.
source: All chimeras localized to the plasma membrane when co-expressed with PC-2F604P (Figure 2B and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and D.

claim: PC-1ΔNT resulted in the strongest surface staining, likely due to the smaller size of this protein.
source: PC-1ΔNT resulted in the strongest surface staining, likely due to the smaller size of this protein.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and the known size difference.

claim: Only sPC-1L31NT/PC-2F604P generated small but appreciable outward currents (35.9 ± 12.9 pA/pF, n = 5).
source: Of the three chimeras, only sPC-1L31NT/PC-2F604P generated small but appreciable outward currents (35.9 ± 12.9 pA/pF, n = 5).
evidence: This is supported by whole cell patch clamp data shown in Figure 2C and E.

claim: Currents in cells expressing sPC-11L3NT/PC-2F604P (9.1 ± 1.9 pA/pF, n = 10) were negligible.
source: Currents in cells expressing sPC-11L3NT/PC-2F604P (9.1 ± 1.9 pA/pF, n = 10) and PC-1ΔNT/PC-2F604P (7.6 ± 1.5 pA/pF, n = 10) were negligible (Figure 2C and E).
evidence: This is supported by whole cell patch clamp data shown in Figure 2C and E.

claim: Currents in cells expressing PC-1ΔNT/PC-2F604P (7.6 ± 1.5 pA/pF, n = 10) were negligible.
source: Currents in cells expressing sPC-11L3NT/PC-2F604P (9.1 ± 1.9 pA/pF, n = 10) and PC-1ΔNT/PC-2F604P (7.6 ± 1.5 pA/pF, n = 10) were negligible (Figure 2C and E).
evidence: This is supported by whole cell patch clamp data shown in Figure 2C and E.

claim: The relative open probability of the sPC-1L31NT/PC-2F604P chimera at −100 mV (0.44 ± 0.0) was ~four-fold higher than sPC-1/PC-2F604P (0.1 ± 0.0).
source: Furthermore, the relative open probability of the sPC-1L31NT/PC-2F604P chimera at −100 mV (0.44 ± 0.0) was ~four-fold higher than sPC-1/PC-2F604P (0.1 ± 0.0) and similar to that for sPC-1pore/PC-2F604P (0.3 ± 0.0) (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by whole cell patch clamp data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The predicted ion permeation region of PC-1L3 does not contain the positively charged amino acids found in PC-1.
source: Interestingly, the predicted ion permeation region of PC-1L3 does not contain the positively charged amino acids found in PC-1, offering a possible explanation for the greater open probability observed in the sPC-1L31NT/PC-2F604P chimeras (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The N-terminus of PC-1 is a key determinant of polycystin complex activation.
source: In terms of channel regulation, these results support the hypothesis that the N-terminus of PC-1 is a key determinant of polycystin complex activation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the chimera experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: sPC-1L31CTL/PC-2F604P generated robust outward currents (87.5 ± 9.0 pA/pF, n = 5).
source: sPC-1L31CTL/PC-2F604P generated robust outward currents (87.5 ± 9.0 pA/pF, n = 5) (Figure 2C and G)
evidence: This is supported by whole cell patch clamp data shown in Figure 2C and G.

claim: The inverse chimera (sPC-11L3CTL) produced only minimal currents (9.1 ± 1.9 pA/pF, n = 10).
source: sPC-1L31CTL/PC-2F604P generated robust outward currents (87.5 ± 9.0 pA/pF, n = 5) (Figure 2C and G) whereas the inverse chimera (sPC-11L3CTL) produced only minimal currents (9.1 ± 1.9 pA/pF, n = 10).
evidence: This is supported by whole cell patch clamp data shown in Figure 2C and G.

claim: The PC-1 CTL domain is essential to activate the polycystin complex.
source: These data strongly suggest that the PC-1 CTL domain is essential to activate the polycystin complex.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the CTL domain swap experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: The PC-1 ectodomain undergoes at least one proteolytic cleavage event at the GPS site in mammalian cells.
source: In mammalian cells, the PC-1 ectodomain undergoes at least one proteolytic cleavage event at the GPS site, suggesting that the N-terminus might be liberated as a secreted ligand.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PC-1 processing.

claim: PC-1 N-terminus-containing exosomes interact with primary cilia in kidney nephrons.
source: Indeed, it has been reported that PC-1 N-terminus-containing exosomes interact with primary cilia in kidney nephrons (Hogan et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: Application of NTF24-852 conferred the ability to carry outward currents on PC-1ΔNT/PC-2F604P heteromers (65.5 ± 37.2 pA/pF, n = 6).
source: Surprisingly, application of an NTF spanning the distal region AA 24–852 (NTF24-852), including the CTL domain between PKD I and II (amino acids 415–531; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C), conferred the ability to carry outward currents on PC-1ΔNT/PC-2F604P heteromers (65.5 ± 37.2 pA/pF, n = 6) (Figure 3A and C).
evidence: This is supported by whole cell patch clamp data shown in Figure 3A and C.

claim: NTF263-535 was able to induce outward currents (61.4 ± 10.5 pA/pF, n = 4) in PC-1ΔNT/PC-2F604P heteromers.
source: Similarly, a shorter NTF containing the CTL domain (NTF263-535; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C) was also able to induce outward currents (61.4 ± 10.5 pA/pF, n = 4; Figures 3A, B and C).
evidence: This is supported by whole cell patch clamp data shown in Figures 3A, B and C.

claim: Boiling NTF263-535 at 95°C for 10 min rendered it inactive.
source: Boiling NTF263-535 at 95°C for 10 min rendered it inactive (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by whole cell patch clamp data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Acute application of NTF263-535 increased current density in PC-1ΔNT/PC-2F604P-expressing cells by 765.1 ± 185.05% (from 5.9 ± 1.3 pA/pF to 59.1 ± 19.3 pA/pF, n = 7) within 10 s.
source: While PC-1ΔNT/PC-2F604P channels remained inactive in the absence of NTF263-535, acute application increased current density by 765.1 ± 185.05% (from 5.9 ± 1.3 pA/pF to 59.1 ± 19.3 pA/pF, n = 7) within 10 s of application (Figures 3D, F and G).
evidence: This is supported by whole cell patch clamp data shown in Figures 3D, F and G.

claim: Non-transfected cells did not respond to NTF263-535 (4.6 ± 1.6 pA/pF to 6.8 ± 1.4 pA/pF, n = 9).
source: However, non-transfected cells did not respond to NTF263-535 under comparable condition (4.6 ± 1.6 pA/pF to 6.8 ± 1.4 pA/pF, n = 9) (Figure 3E and G).
evidence: This is supported by whole cell patch clamp data shown in Figure 3E and G.

claim: Perfusion with 0.125% trypsin decreased sPC-1/PC-2F604P dependent currents by 78.4 ± 4.9% (from 52.0 ± 17.1 pA/pF to 8.9 ± 1.4 pA/pF, n = 6).
source: As shown in Figure 3H perfusion with 0.125% trypsin decreased sPC-1/PC-2F604P dependent currents by 78.4 ± 4.9% (from 52.0 ± 17.1 pA/pF to 8.9 ± 1.4 pA/pF, n = 6, Figure 3H and J, and K).
evidence: This is supported by whole cell patch clamp data shown in Figure 3H, J, and K.

claim: Untransfected cells did not respond to 0.125% trypsin (7.2 ± 1.9 pA/pF versus 4.6 ± 0.8 pA/pF, n = 5).
source: By contrast, untransfected cells did not respond to 0.125% trypsin (7.2 ± 1.9 pA/pF versus 4.6 ± 0.8 pA/pF, n = 5).
evidence: This is supported by whole cell patch clamp data.

claim: The N-terminus including the CTL of PC-1 is necessary and sufficient to activate the polycystin complex.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that the N-terminus including the CTL of PC-1 is necessary and sufficient to activate the polycystin complex.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the NTF application and trypsin experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: The TOP domain in PC-2 forms a bridge between the pore domain and voltage sensor-like domain.
source: We reasoned that the TOP domain in PC-2 is well positioned to function as a surface receptor as it forms a bridge between the pore domain and voltage sensor-like domain, and is critical for channel activation (Shen et al., 2016; Vien et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural and functional studies.

claim: The TOP domain in PC-2 is critical for channel activation.
source: We reasoned that the TOP domain in PC-2 is well positioned to function as a surface receptor as it forms a bridge between the pore domain and voltage sensor-like domain, and is critical for channel activation (Shen et al., 2016; Vien et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Different glycosylation patterns of the TOP domain might underlie conformational changes in the homomeric PC-2 complex.
source: In addition, different glycosylation patterns of the TOP domain might underlie conformational changes in the homomeric PC-2 complex (Wilkes et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: The TOP domain in PC-2 is prominently glycosylated at position N375, N362, and N328.
source: We observed prominent glycosylation of the TOP domain in PC-2 at position N375, N362, and N328 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Mutation of N375 to glutamine did not affect surface localization of sPC-1/PC-2F604PN375Q.
source: Moreover, although mutation of N375 to glutamine did not affect surface localization of sPC-1/PC-2F604PN375Q (Figure 4B and C), it rendered the channel inactive (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: Mutation of N375 to glutamine rendered the sPC-1/PC-2F604PN375Q channel inactive.
source: Moreover, although mutation of N375 to glutamine did not affect surface localization of sPC-1/PC-2F604PN375Q (Figure 4B and C), it rendered the channel inactive (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: This is supported by whole cell patch clamp data shown in Figure 4D and E.

claim: Glycosylation of the TOP domain in PC-2 appears to be required for CTL-dependent polycystin activation.
source: Thus, glycosylation of the TOP domain in PC-2 appears to be required for CTL-dependent polycystin activation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the N375Q mutation data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Single channel openings were readily detected at potentials more positive than +60 mV and more negative than −80 mV in 7 out of 38 wt mIMCD3 cilia.
source: Without any NTFs, we readily detected single channel openings at potentials more positive than +60 mV and more negative than −80 mV (Figure 5A) in 7 out of 38 cilia.
evidence: This is supported by ciliary patch clamp data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Ciliary channels remained readily detectable in 4 of 13 PC-1 knockout cilia.
source: After ablating PC-1 expression in mIMCD3 cells using CRISPR/CAS9 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) ciliary channels remained readily detectable in 4 of 13 cilia (Figure 5B), in agreement with previous reports (Liu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by ciliary patch clamp data shown in Figure 5B and citation to a prior study.

claim: Single channel conductance was comparable between wt mIMCD3 (γ = 79.5 ± 0.1 pS) and PC-1 knockout cilia (γ = 82.3 ± 0.0 pS).
source: In addition, single channel conductance was comparable between wt mIMCD3 (γ = 79.5 ± 0.1 pS) and PC-1 knockout cilia (γ = 82.3 ± 0.0 pS) (Figure 5—figure supplements 1G, H, 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by ciliary patch clamp data shown in Figure 5—figure supplements 1G, H, 2A and B.

claim: The open probability of channels at negative membrane potentials in PC-1 knock out primary cilia (0.58 ± 0.01) was higher than in wt IMCD3 cilia (0.08 ± 0.01).
source: However, we noted that the open probability of channels at negative membrane potentials in PC-1 knock out primary cilia (0.58 ± 0.01) was higher than in wt IMCD3 cilia (0.08 ± 0.01) (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by ciliary patch clamp data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: PC-2 forms a homomeric complex in the absence of PC-1 subunits with a higher open probability than that of PC-1/PC-2 heteromers.
source: These data suggest that PC-2 forms a homomeric complex in the absence of PC-1 subunits with a higher open probability than that of PC-1/PC-2 heteromers.
evidence: This is inferred from the open probability differences between wt and PC-1 knockout cilia shown in Figure 5G.

claim: PC-1 subunits impede cation flux across the membrane.
source: The results also support the idea that PC-1 subunits impede cation flux across the membrane, in agreement with our PC-1 pore mutant data (Figure 1I–K).
evidence: This is inferred from the open probability data and supported by the pore mutant data shown in Figure 1I–K.

claim: Ablation of PC-2 expression using CRISPR/CAS9 rendered primary cilia electrically silent (n = 11).
source: Ablation of PC-2 expression using CRISPR/CAS9 rendered primary cilia electrically silent (n = 11), confirming that PC-2 subunits are an essential component of polycystin channels (Figure 5C; Liu et al., 2018; Kleene and Kleene, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by ciliary patch clamp data shown in Figure 5C and citations to prior studies.

claim: PC-2 subunits are an essential component of polycystin channels.
source: Ablation of PC-2 expression using CRISPR/CAS9 rendered primary cilia electrically silent (n = 11), confirming that PC-2 subunits are an essential component of polycystin channels (Figure 5C; Liu et al., 2018; Kleene and Kleene, 2017).
evidence: This is confirmed by the lack of currents in PC-2 knockout cilia shown in Figure 5C and supported by citations.

claim: NTF263-535 increased the probability of single channel openings by ~five-fold in primary cilia.
source: Although the percentage of electrically active cilia (n = 4/13) remained largely unaffected, NTF263-535 increased the probability of single channels openings by ~five-fold and significantly prolonged the duration of channel openings at negative membrane potentials (Figure 5E–G).
evidence: This is supported by ciliary patch clamp data shown in Figure 5E–G.

claim: NTF263-535 significantly prolonged the duration of channel openings at negative membrane potentials in primary cilia.
source: Although the percentage of electrically active cilia (n = 4/13) remained largely unaffected, NTF263-535 increased the probability of single channels openings by ~five-fold and significantly prolonged the duration of channel openings at negative membrane potentials (Figure 5E–G).
evidence: This is supported by ciliary patch clamp data shown in Figure 5E–G.

claim: PC-2 subunits are essential for functional polycystin channels in primary cilia.
source: Collectively, these findings demonstrate that PC-2 subunits are essential for functional polycystin channels in primary cilia, that PC-1 subunits also participate in the native heteromeric complex, and that NTF263-535 can activate this complex under physiological conditions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ciliary patch clamp experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: PC-1 subunits participate in the native heteromeric complex in primary cilia.
source: Collectively, these findings demonstrate that PC-2 subunits are essential for functional polycystin channels in primary cilia, that PC-1 subunits also participate in the native heteromeric complex, and that NTF263-535 can activate this complex under physiological conditions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ciliary patch clamp experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: NTF263-535 can activate the native polycystin complex under physiological conditions.
source: Collectively, these findings demonstrate that PC-2 subunits are essential for functional polycystin channels in primary cilia, that PC-1 subunits also participate in the native heteromeric complex, and that NTF263-535 can activate this complex under physiological conditions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ciliary patch clamp experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: Currents were not measurable in mIMCD-3 wt cilia under conditions in which Ca2+ is the sole charge carrier, even at very negative membrane potentials (−140 mV).
source: We initially attempted single channel recordings from mIMCD-3 wt cilia under conditions in which Ca2+ is the sole charge carrier (see Materials and methods). We were unable to measure currents, even at very negative membrane potentials (−140 mV) (Figure 6A), in agreement with previously published results (Liu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by ciliary patch clamp data shown in Figure 6A and citation to a prior study.

claim: Application of NTF263-535 revealed channel openings close to physiological membrane potentials when Ca2+ is the sole charge carrier.
source: Surprisingly, however, the application of NTF263-535 revealed channel openings close to physiological membrane potentials (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by ciliary patch clamp data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Single channel conductance was smaller when using Ca2+ instead of Na+ and K+ as the charge carrier (47.5 pS).
source: Single channel conductance was smaller when using Ca2+ instead of Na+ and K+ as the charge carrier (47.5 pS, Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by ciliary patch clamp data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Voltage-dependent open probability and open time remained unchanged when using Ca2+ instead of Na+ and K+ as the charge carrier.
source: Voltage-dependent open probability and open time remained unchanged (Figure 6D and E).
evidence: This is supported by ciliary patch clamp data shown in Figure 6D and E.

claim: Application of NTF263-535 generated multiple rapid spike-like elevations of [Ca2+]cilium (ΔF/F > 0.35, n = 35 cilia).
source: Application of NTF263-535 generated multiple rapid spike-like elevations of [Ca2+]cilium (ΔF/F > 0.35, n = 35 cilia) whereas untreated cells (n = 22) and cells treated with boiled NTF263-535 (n = 28) did not exhibit such fluctuations (Figure 6F and G).
evidence: This is supported by TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 6F and G.

claim: Untreated cells (n = 22) did not exhibit [Ca2+]cilium fluctuations.
source: Application of NTF263-535 generated multiple rapid spike-like elevations of [Ca2+]cilium (ΔF/F > 0.35, n = 35 cilia) whereas untreated cells (n = 22) and cells treated with boiled NTF263-535 (n = 28) did not exhibit such fluctuations (Figure 6F and G).
evidence: This is supported by TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 6F and G.

claim: Cells treated with boiled NTF263-535 (n = 28) did not exhibit [Ca2+]cilium fluctuations.
source: Application of NTF263-535 generated multiple rapid spike-like elevations of [Ca2+]cilium (ΔF/F > 0.35, n = 35 cilia) whereas untreated cells (n = 22) and cells treated with boiled NTF263-535 (n = 28) did not exhibit such fluctuations (Figure 6F and G).
evidence: This is supported by TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 6F and G.

claim: NTF263-535 did not elicit [Ca2+]cilium fluctuations in PC-2 knockout cells (n = 15).
source: In addition, NTF263-535 did not elicit [Ca2+]cilium fluctuations in PC-2 knockout cells (n = 15; Figure 6H and I).
evidence: This is supported by TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 6H and I.

claim: Polycystin channels conduct Ca2+ when activated by NTF263-535.
source: These results show that polycystin channels conduct Ca2+ when activated by NTF263-535.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Ca2+ imaging experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: PC-1 and related family members form a functional ion channel with PC-2.
source: We have demonstrated that PC-1 and related family members form a functional ion channel with PC-2.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Heteromeric PC-1/PC-2 complexes exhibit distinct biophysical properties.
source: These heteromeric complexes exhibit distinct biophysical properties, suggesting that PC-1 members are critical for adjusting the electrical excitability of primary cilia in response to the local environment.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing different properties for different PC-1 family members.

claim: PC-1 members are critical for adjusting the electrical excitability of primary cilia in response to the local environment.
source: These heteromeric complexes exhibit distinct biophysical properties, suggesting that PC-1 members are critical for adjusting the electrical excitability of primary cilia in response to the local environment.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the observed biophysical differences.

claim: The PC-1 N-terminus is essential for the activation of complexes containing PC-2 subunits, including those carrying the gain of function mutation F604P.
source: By expressing membrane-targeted PC-1 or PC-1L3 with PC-2 in mammalian cells, we show that the PC-1 N-terminus is essential for the activation of complexes containing PC-2 subunits, including those carrying the gain of function mutation F604P.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: The CTL domain within the N-terminus of PC-1 is essential for channel activation.
source: More specifically, we show that the CTL domain within the N-terminus of PC-1 is essential for channel activation and that it might function by interacting with the TOP domain of PC-2.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in Figures 2, 3, and 4.

claim: The CTL domain might function by interacting with the TOP domain of PC-2.
source: More specifically, we show that the CTL domain within the N-terminus of PC-1 is essential for channel activation and that it might function by interacting with the TOP domain of PC-2.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism based on the experimental data presented in Figure 4.

claim: An N-terminal fragment containing the CTL domain is sufficient to activate endogenous Ca2+-permeable polycystin channels in cilia.
source: In cilia, we provide evidence that an N-terminal fragment containing the CTL domain is sufficient to activate endogenous Ca2+-permeable polycystin channels and elevate [Ca2+]cilium.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: An N-terminal fragment containing the CTL domain can elevate [Ca2+]cilium.
source: In cilia, we provide evidence that an N-terminal fragment containing the CTL domain is sufficient to activate endogenous Ca2+-permeable polycystin channels and elevate [Ca2+]cilium.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in Figure 6.

claim: The N-terminus of PC-1 activates the channel it is attached to or channels on adjacent cilia following cleavage to become a soluble ligand.
source: Thus, we suggest a novel autoregulation mechanism in which the N-terminus of PC-1 activates the channel it is attached to or channels on adjacent cilia following cleavage to become a soluble ligand.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental findings.

claim: The CTL domain is a hotspot for ADPKD-causing mutations.
source: Our data identify PC-1's CTL domain as an essential component for polycystin activation. Interestingly, the CTL domain is a hotspot for ADPKD-causing mutations (Dong et al., 2019), supporting the critical importance of this domain (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a mutation database study and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: C-type lectins are the most diverse family of mammalian carbohydrate-binding proteins.
source: Although C-type lectins are the most diverse family of mammalian carbohydrate-binding proteins (Keller and Rademacher, 2020), little is known about the function of the CTL motif within PC-1 (Sandford et al., 1997), but it has been reported to bind to carbohydrates in a calcium-dependent manner (Weston et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The CTL motif within PC-1 has been reported to bind to carbohydrates in a calcium-dependent manner.
source: Although C-type lectins are the most diverse family of mammalian carbohydrate-binding proteins (Keller and Rademacher, 2020), little is known about the function of the CTL motif within PC-1 (Sandford et al., 1997), but it has been reported to bind to carbohydrates in a calcium-dependent manner (Weston et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: All PC-1 family members except PC-1L1 contain an N-terminal CTL.
source: All PC-1 family members except PC-1L1 contain an N-terminal CTL, yet PC-1L3 CTL fails to activate the complex.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of PC-1 family member domain structure.

claim: PC-1L3 CTL fails to activate the complex.
source: All PC-1 family members except PC-1L1 contain an N-terminal CTL, yet PC-1L3 CTL fails to activate the complex.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The CTL amino acid sequence diverges between different PC-1s.
source: Because the CTL amino acid sequence diverges between different PC-1s, we speculate that each binds to different carbohydrates.
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Each PC-1 family member CTL may bind to different carbohydrates.
source: Because the CTL amino acid sequence diverges between different PC-1s, we speculate that each binds to different carbohydrates.
evidence: This is speculation based on the sequence divergence.

claim: The CTL domain in the native PC-1/PC-2 complex may interact with glycans in the TOP domain.
source: We speculate that the CTL domain in the native PC-1/PC-2 complex interacts with glycans in the TOP domain, which allosterically regulates the ion permeation pathway and/or gating apparatus of the heteromeric polycystin channel (Vien et al., 2020; Figure 7).
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental findings and illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: Interaction of the CTL domain with glycans in the TOP domain may allosterically regulate the ion permeation pathway and/or gating apparatus of the heteromeric polycystin channel.
source: We speculate that the CTL domain in the native PC-1/PC-2 complex interacts with glycans in the TOP domain, which allosterically regulates the ion permeation pathway and/or gating apparatus of the heteromeric polycystin channel (Vien et al., 2020; Figure 7).
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental findings and illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: The N-glycan attached to N375 of PC-2 is adjacent to a structure that extends above TM3 and TM4 of the voltage sensor-like domain.
source: In particular, the N-glycan attached to N375 of PC-2 is adjacent to a structure that extends above TM3 and TM4 of the voltage sensor-like domain, so it is conceivable that binding of the CTL domain to this glycan will initiate conformational changes in the voltage sensor-like domain, which could be transmitted to the pore to regulate ion permeation.
evidence: This is based on structural knowledge of PC-2.

claim: Binding of the CTL domain to the N-glycan at N375 may initiate conformational changes in the voltage sensor-like domain, which could be transmitted to the pore to regulate ion permeation.
source: In particular, the N-glycan attached to N375 of PC-2 is adjacent to a structure that extends above TM3 and TM4 of the voltage sensor-like domain, so it is conceivable that binding of the CTL domain to this glycan will initiate conformational changes in the voltage sensor-like domain, which could be transmitted to the pore to regulate ion permeation.
evidence: This is speculation based on structural considerations and the N375Q mutation data.

claim: Plasma membrane-targeted polycystins recapitulate biophysical features of ciliary currents.
source: A careful comparison of our ciliary recordings of endogenous polycystin channels with membrane-targeted polycystins reveals that both channel populations exhibit comparable biophysical characteristics, lending weight to the effectiveness of our plasma membrane expression system for studying polycystins.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the experimental data from plasma membrane and ciliary recordings.

claim: The F604P substitution within S5 of PC-2 is thought to induce conformational changes in the S4-S5 linker that lock PC-2 in an open state.
source: It is thought that the F604P substitution within S5 induces conformational changes in the S4-S5 linker (Zheng et al., 2018) that lock PC-2 in an open state.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: Proline substitutions in the S5 segment of several other TRP family members result in constitutive channel activity.
source: Indeed, proline substitutions in the S5 segment of several other TRP family members result in constitutive channel activity (Grimm et al., 2007; Xu et al., 2007; Zhou et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Currents recorded from PC-1 knockout cilia are likely due to homotetrameric PC-2 channels.
source: We speculate that currents recorded from PC-1 knockout cilia are due to homotetrameric PC-2 channels, although we cannot exclude a contribution from other PC-2-containing heteromeric channels such as PC-1L1/PC-2, PC-1L3/PC-2, or PC-2/TRPM3 (Field et al., 2011; DeCaen et al., 2013; Flannery et al., 2015; Bai et al., 2008; Kleene et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental data and supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The native PC-1/PC-2 heteromeric channel in wt cilia showed very short channel openings compared to the presumably homotetrameric PC-2 channel.
source: We noted two striking differences between channels in wt and PC-1 knockout mIMCD-3 cilia at voltages close to the resting membrane potential (DeCaen et al., 2013). First, the native PC-1/PC-2 heteromeric channel in wt cilia showed very short channel openings compared to the presumably homotetrameric PC-2 channel, supporting the hypothesis raised by cryo-EM data that PC-1 reduces ion flux (Su et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 5 and citation to a cryo-EM study.

claim: wt IMCD-3 cilia were electrically silent between membrane potentials of −60 mV and +40 mV.
source: Second, wt IMCD-3 cilia were electrically silent between membrane potentials of −60 mV and +40 mV whereas channels in PC-1 knockout cilia opened at −40 mV.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Channels in PC-1 knockout cilia opened at −40 mV.
source: Second, wt IMCD-3 cilia were electrically silent between membrane potentials of −60 mV and +40 mV whereas channels in PC-1 knockout cilia opened at −40 mV.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Soluble fragments of PC-1 potentiate endogenous polycystin channels that already contain one PC-1 N-terminus.
source: Our results show that soluble fragments of PC-1 potentiate endogenous polycystin channels that already contain one PC-1 N-terminus.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: All three PC-2 TOP domains may need to be simultaneously engaged by CTL domains in order to trigger a concerted conformational change in their respective voltage sensor-like domains and therefore full channel activation.
source: Given the predicted three PC-2:1 PC-1 stoichiometry of the heteromeric polycystin complex, we hypothesize that possibly all three PC-2 TOP domains need to be simultaneously engaged by CTL domains in order to trigger a concerted conformational change in their respective voltage sensor-like domains and therefore full channel activation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the stoichiometry and experimental findings.

claim: The tethered PC-1 N-terminus in a native heteromeric polycystin complex may be sterically constrained to participate in intramolecular interactions with its core complex.
source: Alternatively, the tethered PC-1 N-terminus in a native heteromeric polycystin complex may be sterically constrained to participate in intramolecular interactions with its core complex, and thus might engage in intermolecular interactions, either between polycystin complexes on one cilium or as a cilia-cilia proximity sensor.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of action.

claim: The tethered PC-1 N-terminus might engage in intermolecular interactions, either between polycystin complexes on one cilium or as a cilia-cilia proximity sensor.
source: Alternatively, the tethered PC-1 N-terminus in a native heteromeric polycystin complex may be sterically constrained to participate in intramolecular interactions with its core complex, and thus might engage in intermolecular interactions, either between polycystin complexes on one cilium or as a cilia-cilia proximity sensor.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of action.

claim: As-yet-unknown proteins and/or small molecule ligands may bind to modules in proximity to or in the CTL domain itself.
source: Alternatively, as-yet-unknown proteins and/or small molecule ligands can bind to modules (such as LRRs) that are in proximity to or in the CTL domain itself.
evidence: This is speculation about additional regulatory mechanisms.

claim: Binding of unknown proteins and/or small molecule ligands might mask the carbohydrate-binding site on the CTL domain and thus add another layer of regulation to the polycystin complex.
source: This might mask the carbohydrate-binding site on the CTL domain and thus add another layer of regulation to the polycystin complex.
evidence: This is speculation about additional regulatory mechanisms.

claim: Other more potent agonists of the polycystin complex may exist.
source: While our results show that CTL is required for channel activation, we cannot exclude the possibility that other more potent agonists of the polycystin complex exist.
evidence: This acknowledges the limitations of the current study.

claim: Transport of PC-1 N-terminal ligands by fluids may underlie the molecular chemosensory mechanism of primary cilia.
source: We speculate that transport of such ligands by fluids may underline the molecular chemosensory mechanism of primary cilia.
evidence: This is speculation about the physiological role of the N-terminal fragments.

claim: Activation of endogenous polycystins by N-terminal fragments of PC-1 increases ciliary [Ca2+] in ~30% of cilia imaged.
source: Our data reveal that activation of endogenous polycystins by N-terminal fragments of PC-1 increases ciliary [Ca2+] in ~30% of cilia imaged.
evidence: This is a summary of the Ca2+ imaging data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Only a fraction of cilia shows electrically active polycystin channels.
source: This is in agreement with previously published work in which only a fraction of cilia shows electrically active polycystin channels.
evidence: This is supported by prior literature.
